screens.title: Singleton Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the Singleton pattern and why it appears so often in C# applications. The Singleton's goal is simple: guarantee a single instance of a class and provide a global access point. That single instance is useful for managing shared resources such as a database connection pool, a centralized configuration loader, or a logging service writing to one file. You will learn the core mechanism — a private constructor, a static field that holds the instance, and a public static accessor — and then we will examine thread-safety techniques that matter in multi-threaded applications. Along the way we'll compare an unsafe, simple implementation with the safer double-checked locking approach and the idiomatic Lazy solution. We will also discuss when Singleton becomes a liability: overuse, tight coupling, and testing difficulty. By the end of the chapter you'll understand how to implement a Logger or ConfigurationManager safely, why Lazy is preferred in modern C#, and what questions to ask before choosing Singleton over dependency injection. Consider: does this service truly need a single instance for the lifetime of the application?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Singleton Pattern
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Singleton Pattern

Guarantee a single instance and a global access point for shared resources.

In this lesson
Implement single-instance classes, learn thread-safety, and build a Logger example.
Why it matters
Avoid resource contention and inconsistent state when multiple parts of an app share a service.
Coming up
Non-thread-safe pitfalls, lock-based fixes, and the Lazy<T> approach.
Explore Key Topics
Purpose & Use Cases
When a single instance simplifies resource management.
Thread Safety
Locking vs Lazy<T> strategies for concurrent access.
Pitfalls & Testing
Why excessive singletons create tight coupling and testing pain.
This chapter uses compact code examples and a hands-on logger activity to demonstrate safe implementations. Expect clear comparisons and a short checklist to judge whether Singleton is appropriate for a given service.
Visual Concept
Single instance
Private constructor + static accessor
Thread safety
Locking or Lazy<T> to avoid race conditions
Tip: Ask whether dependency injection could provide the same single instance with better testability.
Starter activity
Implement the provided Logger using Lazy<T> and run a small threaded test. Confirm initialization runs exactly once.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your attention on practical skills and sound judgment. First, you'll understand the purpose and benefits of the Singleton pattern in C# applications, including why a single instance can help manage shared resources and avoid duplicated work. Second, you'll implement thread-safe Singletons using established techniques: using the lock keyword with double-checked locking, and the idiomatic Lazy approach that defers creation until first access. Third, you'll learn to recognize when Singleton is appropriate — for example, a centralized logging utility or a configuration manager — and when it introduces tight coupling that harms testability. Finally, you'll identify common mistakes like over-using Singleton or loading unrelated responsibilities into a single class. Each objective ties a practical skill to a why: how it affects concurrency, resource usage, and maintainability. By the end you'll be able to implement a Logger Singleton and evaluate whether dependency injection might be a better fit. Think of these goals as both coding skills and design judgment you'll practice in exercises and examples.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Skill Focus
Practical checklist
  1. Make the constructor private so external code cannot create instances directly.
  2. Provide a static field to hold the instance and a public static accessor.
  3. Choose a thread-safety strategy: lock/double-check or Lazy<T> for idiomatic C#.
  4. Keep Singletons narrow in responsibility to avoid violating Single Responsibility Principle.
  5. Consider dependency injection when testability and flexibility matter more than a global access point.
Try this

After implementing the Logger, remove the private constructor and observe why external code can now create multiple instances. This demonstrates how the private constructor enforces uniqueness.

Quick mnemonic
Think: PRIVATE constructor, STATIC holder, PUBLIC accessor. Repeat: create once, provide globally.

screens.title: What the Singleton Pattern Is
screens.narratorSegment: The Singleton pattern is a creational pattern that enforces a single instance of a class and offers a global access point to it. At its core, a Singleton performs three responsibilities: prevent external construction by making the constructor private, hold the single instance in a static field, and provide a public static accessor that returns the same object on every call. This combination gives code a reliable, shared object to manage application-wide concerns. Concrete situations include a configuration manager that reads app settings once and serves them to the whole app, a logging service that serializes writes to one file, or a connection pool controller that avoids creating duplicate connections. A common misconception is that Singleton merely means a global variable; the critical difference is that the Singleton also controls instantiation and lifecycle. Another misconception is assuming Singleton solves all sharing problems; in multi-threaded applications we must ensure the accessor creates the instance safely or we risk multiple instances. As an example, consider a configuration manager that loads settings at startup. Using a Singleton prevents multiple loads and keeps the configuration consistent across modules. Ask yourself: does this service really need application-wide uniqueness, or could scoped services and dependency injection offer better testability?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What the Singleton Is
Definition

Singleton: single instance and global access

A class enforces a single instance, preventing multiple constructions and offering a single point of access across the app.

Everyday examples
Configuration manager, logging service, connection pool controller.
Common misconception
Singleton is not just a global variable; it controls instantiation and lifecycle.
Why it matters
Prevents duplicate resource initialization and ensures consistent shared state when used correctly.
Visual summary
Responsibilities
  • Private constructor to block external new.
  • Static field to hold the instance.
  • Public static accessor to return the instance.
Concrete scenario
A ConfigurationManager loads settings once at initialization and serves read access to many modules, avoiding repeated file reads.
Key Takeaway

Singleton centralizes ownership of a single instance; use it when application-wide uniqueness is required and manage concurrency carefully.

screens.title: Core Implementation Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing a Singleton in C# follows a compact set of steps, each with a reason. Step one: make the constructor private so no external code can call new and create additional instances. This enforces control over how instances are created. Step two: add a static field inside the class to hold the single instance. Because static fields belong to the type rather than an object, the instance lives at the application level. Step three: expose a public static property or method that returns the single instance. That accessor is the global point of access for the rest of your code. Together, these steps guarantee control over creation and provide a predictable access path. A useful practical check is to attempt new from client code: if the constructor is private, compilation fails and you have enforced the rule. Another important detail is when and how the static field is initialized: eager initialization creates the instance at type load, lazy initialization delays creation until first use, and thread safety considerations determine whether simple checks are sufficient. Always keep responsibilities focused: the Singleton should not become a catch-all for unrelated functionality.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Implementation Steps
Process

Three-step recipe

1. Private constructor
Prevents external code from calling new and enforces controlled instantiation.
2. Static instance field
Holds the single instance at the type level so it's shared across the application.
3. Public static accessor
Provides a global point of access and controls lazy or eager creation of the instance.
Concrete Example
public sealed class ConfigurationManager
{
  private static ConfigurationManager _instance;
  private ConfigurationManager() { /* load settings */ }
  public static ConfigurationManager Instance
  {
    get
    {
      if (_instance == null)
      {
        _instance = new ConfigurationManager();
      }
      return _instance;
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

These three structural elements enforce uniqueness and provide controlled global access when used together.

screens.title: A Non-Thread-Safe Singleton
screens.narratorSegment: Let's inspect a simple non-thread-safe Singleton implementation and see how it can fail. The common pattern uses a private constructor, a private static field, and a public static Instance property that checks if the field is null and then instantiates. This works in single-threaded code, but in a multi-threaded environment two threads can simultaneously observe the field as null and both proceed to create an instance. The result is two distinct objects, violating the Singleton guarantee. In practice, this can cause inconsistent settings, duplicated resource initialization, or file access conflicts when both instances try to manage the same external resource. The code example shown is typical for a ConfigurationManager: a dictionary of settings is loaded in the constructor, and the Instance accessor lazily creates the manager. To observe the failure, run the code in a multi-threaded test where several threads request the Instance at startup; if initialization runs more than once, you have a race condition. The immediate fix is to synchronize creation with locks, but that introduces performance considerations and requires careful implementation like double-checked locking. Recognize the problem early by running concurrent tests that access the accessor simultaneously.

keyIdea.title: Race condition risk
keyIdea.text: Simple null-check creation is not safe in concurrent scenarios; concurrent threads may create multiple instances.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Non-Thread-Safe Example
Code Walkthrough
public sealed class ConfigurationManager
{
  private static ConfigurationManager _instance;
  private readonly Dictionary<string,string> _settings;

  private ConfigurationManager()
  {
    _settings = new Dictionary<string,string>();
    LoadSettingsFromFile();
    Console.WriteLine("ConfigurationManager instance created.");
  }

  public static ConfigurationManager Instance
  {
    get
    {
      if (_instance == null)
      {
        _instance = new ConfigurationManager();
      }
      return _instance;
    }
  }

  // GetSetting, SetSetting omitted for brevity
}
Explanation
  • The Instance property checks a null field and constructs the object. This is lazy initialization.
  • If two threads enter the check at the same time, both may create a new object, producing two instances.
  • Resulting problems include inconsistent state, duplicate resource operations, and debugging complexity.
Common mistake
Assuming a null check alone guarantees a single instance in multi-threaded settings.
Check your understanding

How would you prove your Instance accessor is thread-safe? Run multiple threads that call Instance concurrently and verify initialization output appears once.

screens.title: Double-Checked Locking with lock
screens.narratorSegment: Double-checked locking is a pattern that combines a quick unsynchronized check with a synchronized block to avoid unnecessary locking after initialization. The property first checks whether the instance is null. Only if it is null does the code acquire a lock on a private static object, then re-check the instance inside the lock and create it if still null. This ensures only one thread actually constructs the object while allowing subsequent reads to avoid the lock path and therefore remain fast. It is important to implement this pattern carefully: the lock object must be private and readonly, and the double-check ensures the instance is created exactly once. While double-checked locking reduces lock contention compared to locking on every access, it adds complexity and can be error-prone in some memory models if not used properly. For these reasons, many C# developers prefer the simpler and safer Lazy approach. Still, double-checked locking is a useful pattern to understand when you need fine-grained control over synchronization and performance trade-offs. Double-Checked Locking with lock means use an initial null check, a lock, and a second null check to safely create the instance with minimal locking overhead.. In practical terms, reduce locking overhead while ensuring safe initialization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Double-Checked Locking
Pattern code
public sealed class ThreadSafeConfigurationManager
{
  private static ThreadSafeConfigurationManager _instance;
  private static readonly object _lock = new object();

  private ThreadSafeConfigurationManager() { /* load settings */ }

  public static ThreadSafeConfigurationManager Instance
  {
    get
    {
      if (_instance == null)
      {
        lock (_lock)
        {
          if (_instance == null)
          {
            _instance = new ThreadSafeConfigurationManager();
          }
        }
      }
      return _instance;
    }
  }
}
Why it helps
  • First check avoids the lock once initialization completes, improving performance for subsequent calls.
  • The lock protects the critical section so only one thread constructs the instance.
  • The second check inside the lock prevents duplicate construction if multiple threads reached the lock.
Pitfall to watch
Implementing the checks or lock incorrectly can still result in race conditions. Memory model subtleties make this pattern trickier than it looks.
Pro tip

Prefer Lazy<T> in modern C# unless you require this explicit control for performance or platform reasons.

screens.title: Using Lazy<T> for Thread-Safe Lazy Initialization
screens.narratorSegment: The Lazy class in. NET provides a simple, robust way to implement lazy, thread-safe initialization without manually writing locks. Lazy encapsulates the logic needed to create the instance on first access and ensures thread safety according to the chosen LazyThreadSafetyMode. The typical implementation defines a readonly static Lazy of the Singleton type and returns its Value property from the public accessor. This approach reduces boilerplate code and avoids subtle race conditions that can occur with manual double-checked locking. It also centralizes the lazy behavior and allows you to pick a thread-safety mode if necessary. For example, defining a private static readonly Lazy<LazyConfigurationManager> field initialized with a lambda that constructs the object ensures the constructor runs only once, even when multiple threads request the Instance simultaneously. Because this is concise and well-tested in the framework, it is generally preferred for modern C# development. Use this approach when you want safe, readable code and you do not need specialized synchronization behavior. Using Lazy<T> for Thread-Safe Lazy Initialization means use lazy<t> to get concise, thread-safe lazy initialization without manual locks.. In practical terms, the preferred, concise pattern in modern .net. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Lazy<T> Example
Code
public sealed class LazyConfigurationManager
{
  private static readonly Lazy<LazyConfigurationManager> _lazyInstance =
    new Lazy<LazyConfigurationManager>(() => new LazyConfigurationManager());

  private LazyConfigurationManager() { /* load settings */ }

  public static LazyConfigurationManager Instance => _lazyInstance.Value;

  // GetSetting, SetSetting omitted
}
Benefits
  • Handles thread-safety and lazy initialization for you.
  • Reduces boilerplate and the risk of subtle errors in locking.
  • Clear and idiomatic in .NET Framework 4 and later.
When to choose it
When you want a concise, safe Singleton and do not need specialized synchronization semantics.
Misconception check

Lazy<T> does not remove the design judgment about whether Singleton is appropriate; it only makes safe creation easier.

screens.title: Singleton for Centralized Logging
screens.narratorSegment: A common, practical use of Singleton is a centralized Logger. A single logging instance prevents multiple threads from opening and writing to the same file independently, which can cause file locks, interleaved writes, or inconsistent timestamps. The starter activity in this chapter provides a Logger class implemented with Lazy and a Program that spawns multiple threads to write messages. The Logger constructor prints an initialization message so you can confirm it runs only once. Each thread calls the Logger. Instance. LogMessage method with sample messages, and when joined you should see the initialization line exactly once followed by the log entries. This demonstrates both lazy initialization and thread safety in practice. When implementing a logger, keep responsibilities limited: the Singleton should manage access to the logging resource, but not also parse business rules or perform unrelated work. For testing, consider abstracting the logging interface so you can replace the Singleton in unit tests, or use dependency injection in larger systems while keeping a single concrete instance registered per application lifetime. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Logger Activity
Starter code (excerpt)
public sealed class Logger
{
  private static readonly Lazy<Logger> _lazyInstance = new Lazy<Logger>(() => new Logger());

  private Logger()
  {
    Console.WriteLine("Logger instance initialized.");
  }

  public static Logger Instance => _lazyInstance.Value;

  public void LogMessage(string message)
  {
    string logEntry = $"{DateTime.Now:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [{Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId}] {message}";
    Console.WriteLine(logEntry);
  }
}
Activity steps
  1. Implement the Logger using the provided Lazy<T> field and private constructor.
  2. Start multiple threads that call Logger.Instance.LogMessage concurrently.
  3. Confirm the initialization message appears exactly once and all messages are logged.
Real-world note
In production, loggers may also perform file I/O, rotation, and buffering. Keep those concerns separate from Singleton instantiation when possible.
Check

If you see the initialization line more than once, your Singleton is not thread-safe or multiple application domains are creating instances.

screens.title: When Singleton Becomes an Anti-Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: While Singleton solves the problem of single shared resources, it can become an anti-pattern when overused or misapplied. The main issues are tight coupling and reduced testability. If many classes directly call Singleton. Instance, those classes become dependent on a global state, making isolated unit tests difficult because you cannot easily substitute a mock. screens.title: A Practical Checklist for Safe Singletons
screens.narratorSegment: Before you commit to a Singleton, run this practical checklist. First, confirm the service truly needs application-wide uniqueness: configuration, shared caches, or a single writer logger are common candidates. Second, keep the Singleton small: one clear responsibility avoids violating the Single Responsibility Principle. Third, choose a thread-safety strategy — Lazy is preferred, but double-checked locking can be used when specialized control is required. Fourth, make the constructor private and the static fields readonly where appropriate to prevent accidental reassignment. Fifth, design for testability: either provide an interface the Singleton implements or prefer dependency injection so you can substitute a test double in unit tests. Sixth, plan lifecycle and disposal if the resource requires cleanup; Singletons long-lived across the application may need explicit disposal hooks. Finally, run concurrency tests: spawn multiple threads that access the Instance concurrently and assert initialization occurs once. Following this checklist reduces the risk that a Singleton becomes a source of bugs or architectural debt. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the Singleton pattern and why it appears so often in C# applications. The Singleton's goal is simple: guarantee a single instance of a class and provide a global access point. That single instance is useful for managing shared resources such as a database connection pool, a centralized configuration loader, or a logging service writing to one file. You will learn the core mechanism — a private constructor, a static field that holds the instance, and a public static accessor — and then we will examine thread-safety techniques that matter in multi-threaded applications. Along the way we'll compare an unsafe, simple implementation with the safer double-checked locking approach and the idiomatic Lazy solution. We will also discuss when Singleton becomes a liability: overuse, tight coupling, and testing difficulty. By the end of the chapter you'll understand how to implement a Logger or ConfigurationManager safely, why Lazy is preferred in modern C#, and what questions to ask before choosing Singleton over dependency injection. Consider: does this service truly need a single instance for the lifetime of the application?

These learning objectives focus your attention on practical skills and sound judgment. First, you'll understand the purpose and benefits of the Singleton pattern in C# applications, including why a single instance can help manage shared resources and avoid duplicated work. Second, you'll implement thread-safe Singletons using established techniques: using the lock keyword with double-checked locking, and the idiomatic Lazy approach that defers creation until first access. Third, you'll learn to recognize when Singleton is appropriate — for example, a centralized logging utility or a configuration manager — and when it introduces tight coupling that harms testability. Finally, you'll identify common mistakes like over-using Singleton or loading unrelated responsibilities into a single class. Each objective ties a practical skill to a why: how it affects concurrency, resource usage, and maintainability. By the end you'll be able to implement a Logger Singleton and evaluate whether dependency injection might be a better fit. Think of these goals as both coding skills and design judgment you'll practice in exercises and examples.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied outcomes and evaluation. You will implement Singleton variants and test them under concurrent access to observe race conditions and correct initialization. You will also learn to evaluate whether a service truly needs a single instance or whether dependency injection is a better tool. Practically, you will complete a hands-on activity: build a Logger Singleton using Lazy, run multiple threads, and verify the initialization message appears once. You will practice code inspection to spot common mistakes such as exposing public constructors or combining unrelated responsibilities. Finally, you will learn a quick checklist for applying Singleton safely: make the constructor private, expose a static accessor, choose a thread-safety strategy, keep responsibilities focused, and consider testability. These are the concrete abilities you will be able to demonstrate in code and code review scenarios by the end of this chapter.

The Singleton pattern is a creational pattern that enforces a single instance of a class and offers a global access point to it. At its core, a Singleton performs three responsibilities: prevent external construction by making the constructor private, hold the single instance in a static field, and provide a public static accessor that returns the same object on every call. This combination gives code a reliable, shared object to manage application-wide concerns. Concrete situations include a configuration manager that reads app settings once and serves them to the whole app, a logging service that serializes writes to one file, or a connection pool controller that avoids creating duplicate connections. A common misconception is that Singleton merely means a global variable; the critical difference is that the Singleton also controls instantiation and lifecycle. Another misconception is assuming Singleton solves all sharing problems; in multi-threaded applications we must ensure the accessor creates the instance safely or we risk multiple instances. As an example, consider a configuration manager that loads settings at startup. Using a Singleton prevents multiple loads and keeps the configuration consistent across modules. Ask yourself: does this service really need application-wide uniqueness, or could scoped services and dependency injection offer better testability?

Implementing a Singleton in C# follows a compact set of steps, each with a reason. Step one: make the constructor private so no external code can call new and create additional instances. This enforces control over how instances are created. Step two: add a static field inside the class to hold the single instance. Because static fields belong to the type rather than an object, the instance lives at the application level. Step three: expose a public static property or method that returns the single instance. That accessor is the global point of access for the rest of your code. Together, these steps guarantee control over creation and provide a predictable access path. A useful practical check is to attempt new from client code: if the constructor is private, compilation fails and you have enforced the rule. Another important detail is when and how the static field is initialized: eager initialization creates the instance at type load, lazy initialization delays creation until first use, and thread safety considerations determine whether simple checks are sufficient. Always keep responsibilities focused: the Singleton should not become a catch-all for unrelated functionality.

Let's inspect a simple non-thread-safe Singleton implementation and see how it can fail. The common pattern uses a private constructor, a private static field, and a public static Instance property that checks if the field is null and then instantiates. This works in single-threaded code, but in a multi-threaded environment two threads can simultaneously observe the field as null and both proceed to create an instance. The result is two distinct objects, violating the Singleton guarantee. In practice, this can cause inconsistent settings, duplicated resource initialization, or file access conflicts when both instances try to manage the same external resource. The code example shown is typical for a ConfigurationManager: a dictionary of settings is loaded in the constructor, and the Instance accessor lazily creates the manager. To observe the failure, run the code in a multi-threaded test where several threads request the Instance at startup; if initialization runs more than once, you have a race condition. The immediate fix is to synchronize creation with locks, but that introduces performance considerations and requires careful implementation like double-checked locking. Recognize the problem early by running concurrent tests that access the accessor simultaneously.

Double-checked locking is a pattern that combines a quick unsynchronized check with a synchronized block to avoid unnecessary locking after initialization. The property first checks whether the instance is null. Only if it is null does the code acquire a lock on a private static object, then re-check the instance inside the lock and create it if still null. This ensures only one thread actually constructs the object while allowing subsequent reads to avoid the lock path and therefore remain fast. It is important to implement this pattern carefully: the lock object must be private and readonly, and the double-check ensures the instance is created exactly once. While double-checked locking reduces lock contention compared to locking on every access, it adds complexity and can be error-prone in some memory models if not used properly. For these reasons, many C# developers prefer the simpler and safer Lazy approach. Still, double-checked locking is a useful pattern to understand when you need fine-grained control over synchronization and performance trade-offs. Double-Checked Locking with lock means use an initial null check, a lock, and a second null check to safely create the instance with minimal locking overhead.. The Lazy class in. NET provides a simple, robust way to implement lazy, thread-safe initialization without manually writing locks. Lazy encapsulates the logic needed to create the instance on first access and ensures thread safety according to the chosen LazyThreadSafetyMode. The typical implementation defines a readonly static Lazy of the Singleton type and returns its Value property from the public accessor. This approach reduces boilerplate code and avoids subtle race conditions that can occur with manual double-checked locking. It also centralizes the lazy behavior and allows you to pick a thread-safety mode if necessary. For example, defining a private static readonly Lazy<LazyConfigurationManager> field initialized with a lambda that constructs the object ensures the constructor runs only once, even when multiple threads request the Instance simultaneously. Because this is concise and well-tested in the framework, it is generally preferred for modern C# development.
